objectives.text: Turn climate finance into a reform of the World Bank and IMF. The Bridgetown Initiative, first set out in 2022 by a group led by Prime Minister Mia Mottley, asks for emergency liquidity against debt crises, about US$1 trillion more multilateral lending for climate and social development, and guarantees to draw private capital into climate projects. Its later version, 3.0, was launched at the Small Island Developing States conference in Antigua and Barbuda.

objectives.text: Keep the Caribbean out of a US military frame. In September 2025 Mottley told the UN General Assembly that the Caribbean 'must remain a zone of peace' and warned that the build-up of military assets 'could occasion just an accident'. In October she called the situation 'extremely dangerous and untenable' and urged regional leaders to reject US strikes on alleged drug traffickers, which she called extrajudicial killings.

means.text: The UN and climate stages. Mottley's General Assembly speech and the Bridgetown name make a small state heard far beyond its size. In the same speech she praised Kenya's leadership of the Haiti security mission and asked the UN Security Council and the OAS for more support.

means.text: The Commonwealth link to London. Barbados became a republic in 2021 but stays in the Commonwealth and keeps a High Commission in London; it is the UK's fourth-largest export market in the Caribbean. The shared history (1627-1966) gives the channel its weight.

constraints.text: A small state asking large shareholders for money. The Bridgetown reform needs the votes and capital of the large economies that run the World Bank and IMF. Its ideas have gained traction among them, but the sources say they are still being debated, and one German-language source calls parts of them contested.

paradoxes.text: Her climate case runs through the institutions whose governance is set by large shareholders, the governments whose military posture she calls 'untenable'. Pressing Washington on the Caribbean build-up while needing its support for the World Bank and IMF reform pulls two ways. This is our reading; no source states the US weight in those votes.

grand_strategy.reading: Barbados under Mottley plays a small state's game: its weight comes from a climate and debt agenda carried through UN and multilateral stages, and from a regional line against militarisation that puts it at odds with the US deployment and with Trinidad and Tobago. Its tie to London is the Commonwealth and history rather than a treaty, and the reparations claim, the China loans, the CARICOM files on Haiti and Venezuela and the weight of tourism are not sourced in this pass. Hurricanes and the debt level, the two constraints a Caribbean card would normally lead with, are also unverified here and stay open until a source is read.

stances.note: Partner, no alliance. Barbados shares history with London (empire to independence in 1966) and stays in the Commonwealth, keeps a High Commission in Bridgetown and London, and is the UK's fourth-largest export market in the Caribbean (Wikipedia). It became a republic in 2021 and the monarch is no longer its head of state. Bond affinity is our reading: shared institutions, no kinship. The reparations claim Mottley has pressed on Britain is not sourced in this pass; if a source confirms it as an open historical wound, the bond becomes grievance. Trend stable is our reading: no source in this pass shows movement. Confidence C: tier 4 Wikipedia only, no UK or Barbadian government statement read.

stances.note: Reluctant partner, our reading of the 2025 posture: Mottley opposes the US naval build-up and the strikes in the southern Caribbean, calling them an accident risk and 'untenable', yet keeps cooperation and no open break, and pushes for dialogue through the UN. The grade follows the structure, not the rhetoric: no alliance binds the two. Trend cooling is our reading of the September and October 2025 statements. Bond none: no kinship or historical grievance named in these sources. Confidence C: tier 3 press only (Barbados Today read in full; the Gleaner and the Caribbean Camera known from search summaries); no Barbadian or US government document read, and no 2026 development found.
